My views on AI have radically shifted over the past few weeks, after spending way too much time reading about it and watching interviews of industry leaders and experts.

First, I really love the tools. I spend $200 on Claude every month and the product is worth every penny for me. Probably even more. I think the existing tools can deliver significant increase to future GDP and help us solve major global challenges faced by humanity.

However, I just cannot comprehend why the industry is not much more regulated, as its leaders and employees seem to request themselves. I meet a lot of people who have heard of the hugging face incident but don’t know the actual chain of events. If you don’t, you definitely should spend a least an hour reading about it.

I also do not know why we need to follow the path that frontier labs are following, to develop ever more powerful models. It seems to me that they are enormous gains that are readily available if we deploy the current technology in economic and scientific organizations without pursuing a super intelligence that they say might kill us and more likely wreak havoc in society. I know a lot of people think these warnings are marketing tricks, and that’s a reasonable assumption. But I don’t see the point of taking such risks.

My median scenario is that of many economists: AI will diffuse slowly and lift gdp growth by a percentage point or so, will cause some economic disruption on the way, but ultimately people will get new jobs and maybe work less.

However, I am deeply uncomfortable with the absolutely wild level of uncertainty around this prediction. And to be honest, even setting the doom scenarios aside, I find the utopia scenarios of some industry leaders actually dystopian. And I think a large majority of the public would agree if they paid attention to what they’re saying. To their credit, they themselves agree publicly that they should not be the ones making these choices. A large majority of the public is now very skeptical of AI as a source of human progress, in particular among younger adults who use it the most. They should have a say.

I don’t want to convince you of anything but to get informed about this topic, express yourself and vote accordingly.

It’s easy to get absorbed in your Claude or Codex terminal right now.

It feels like you can build anything, but it’s also easy to lose track. What’s the direction or purpose? Are we just reacting to things, or do we know where we want to take the company?

“Agents and people are ripping. It’s great, but it’s unclear what value we’re creating.”

We do this at Linear, and keeping a shared picture of the work is how I retain my sanity as things move faster. I do all my AI work inside Linear, connected to this context. I learn, think, write, and adjust plans with a view into what everyone is working on and what they’ve thought about or done in the past.

This is why I think projects, initiatives, and teams become more useful as agents do more of the work. We need ways to give that work context and direction outside of individual agent sessions, and connect the results back to what we’re trying to accomplish.

A project gives whatever you’re building a home: issues, documents, customer feedback, milestones, updates. I make projects even for personal work.

We also use projects to follow adoption metrics and other things we care about as the work progresses. The context, the work, and the evidence stay together, often in a project update I can glance at in the morning.

Teams establish the conventions, triage rules, and automations for how the work happens.

Initiatives give projects a shared direction. Define something you want the company to accomplish, then connect the projects contributing to it. People and agents get the broader context: why their work matters and how they should approach it.

A weekly Loop can pull together progress across those projects, with a person reviewing and adding judgment. Leadership can see what’s happening and adjust the direction.

This was useful before AI. Now, with the right guidance, AI can do a lot of the work of keeping that context current. It makes the work across the company easier to understand, and that understanding informs my own work.

Linear also connects to our internal tools and data sources. I can explore a new area against the history of the product, what we’ve tried before, current data, customer feedback, and ongoing work. Then start a proposal or discussion and adjust our plans.

All of this is available by tagging @linear in Slack or sending it a DM.

This is why company context matters so much to me. Models and harnesses are available to everyone, including through Linear and other tools.

Your people, history, decisions, customers, and current work are specific to your company. Making that knowledge available to the people and agents doing the work helps you build on the advantages you already have.

Police departments and schools can apply for the scanner that reads it, but if you're the one paying Anthropic $20 a month, you're not allowed to run it on your own writing.

The stamp is hidden in which words Claude picks. Every time it chooses a word, it leans a tiny bit toward certain options based on a secret key, and over enough words that adds up to a pattern a scanner can spot. It survives copy and paste. Anthropic says it can survive some editing too.

It also doesn't care how much of the writing was yours. Anthropic's own help page says a hit means Claude touched the text, so a cover letter you wrote at midnight and asked Claude to tighten up can get flagged right alongside one it wrote from scratch. Anthropic even admits a positive result isn't fully conclusive. So you can be judged by a test you're not allowed to take, using a scanner its own maker says can be wrong.

What gets me is that no law made them do this here.

The EU's AI Act requires the stamp inside Europe and stops at the border. A freelancer in Ohio or a college kid in Texas is nowhere near it. OpenAI read the exact same law and only stamps ChatGPT for users in the EU, and everyone else stays unmarked unless a developer turns it on.

OpenAI also knows exactly what this costs. Back in 2024, the Wall Street Journal reported OpenAI had a watermark that caught 99.9% of ChatGPT text and kept it on the shelf anyway. An internal survey found nearly 30% of users would use ChatGPT less if it had a watermark and a competitor didn't, and 69% thought detectors would get people falsely accused.

Anthropic looked at those numbers and signed up to be the competitor with the watermark, worldwide, in places where no law asked for it.

The standard excuse is that a public scanner would teach people how to scrub the stamp. I get that, and it's a fair reason to keep it away from random strangers on the internet. A 1920x1080 flat vector explainer in the style of the big infographic animation channels. Every scene is a full illustrated place (a lab, a street, a classroom, a stage) with characters acting the line out.
Flat colour shapes, no outlines, one slightly darker flat shade for form, a muted palette (dusty blue-grey, slate teal, warm beige, navy, soft purple), salmon-pink skin, big heads, dot eyes.
A new scene every 2-4 s and a hard cut on every sentence that changes the idea. A white splat wipe (0.2 s in, 0.2 s out) between big sections. The camera always drifts 2-4% or pans.
Text lives only on things in the world: signs on posts, hanging boards, chalkboards, building panels and screens.
- It is typed in Montserrat 800 at 26-34 letters a second. Each letter arrives 1.45x big and 0.7 em to the right, then settles in 0.18 s.
- Ink is #2b2d42 on white boards.
- A red X (#d62828, 30 px round strokes, two strokes of 0.11 s each) goes over every wrong idea.
- Every date gets a white 330x120 card top left with an orange #f4a261 calendar.
- Headlines are white 92-96 px caps on a flat colour (#e2552f with drifting lighter puffs, or #5b3fa6 with slowly turning #6a4cb6 gears).
Banned: outlines, motion-design UI floating over the art (code editors, glass cards, checklists), emoji, burned-in subtitles, any channel's logo, a still frame longer than 1 s, and a character who doesn't move.
</direction>

<structure>
Length: the voice decides, 55-65 s at about 190 words per minute.
0 s a second-person hook that flips what the viewer assumes, acted out literally, then a red X on the denial line → 3-8 s the stakes in one shocking true line, with icons popping in one per word → 8-11 s the subject revealed under a spotlight, its name typed on a sign → 11-18 s the origin: the real place with its name typed on its own sign, a date card, people walking in or out of it → 18-24 s the types or parts, landing one by one on their names, each labelled → 24-25.5 s "so how does it work?" as a headline with question marks popping → 25.5-36 s the mechanism acted out in 2-3 places (a chalkboard, a machine, a map), with a counter rolling up to the big number → 36-46 s what it leads to, with characters who react (jump, turn, a "!" pops) → 46-55 s the twist that ties back to the hook → 55 s the last line is a question to the viewer, the viewer character from the hook reacts, and the sign holds to the end.
</structure>

<build>
1. Tools: Python, Playwright with Chromium, FFmpeg, faster-whisper, OpenCV, Pillow, librosa. Install what's missing and tell me what you installed.
2. Art: everything at 3840x2160, with 3-5 frames of the reference channel as style references (crop their logo off first).
   - One EMPTY plate per scene: no people, straight-on, open floor, blank signs and screens to write on in code.
   - Character sheets on solid chroma green #00B140, with nothing green on anyone.
   - Draw any character who gestures a lot WITHOUT ARMS, only round shoulder sockets, so code draws the arms. Draw everyone else in the exact pose their scene needs: side view at a desk, side view walking, seen from behind, sitting.
3. Cutouts:
   - The background is every pixel with G - max(R,B) over 40, within 110 of the median green, connected to the border.
   - Add a 2 px soft alpha band, and clamp G to max(R,B) + 6 inside it.
   - Split heads at the neck, drawing hands, and walkers' legs below the coat hem.
   - Refill each hole with inpainting from the body's own colours (transparent pixels masked too), so a turning piece never shows a gap.
4. Voice:
   - Pick it by measuring median pitch (pyin) and MFCC timbre against a clip of the narrator you want.
   - Generate one take, cut pauses over 0.24 s to 0.16 s, and atempo it to the target length.
   - Get word timestamps with faster-whisper. Every cut, sign and gesture starts on a real word.
5. Film: one HTML canvas where every frame is a pure function of time: window. seek(t), READY, END, and EV with the sound times. One function per shot.
   - Arms: two-bone IK tubes (upper 118, lower 112, 36 thick for a 918 px tall sprite) with mitten hands that open, point or make a fist.
   - Faces blink for 0.14 s every 2.7-4.2 s. Heads nod ±0.035 rad. Drawing hands scribble ±8 px.
   - Walks:
     - Thighs swing ±0.42 rad, and the knee bends 0.75·cos² on the swing.
     - The hips drop so the planted foot stays down.
     - The body moves 1.5 leg lengths per cycle, so feet never slide.
   - Draw each plate inside the same camera transform as everything on it, and clamp the camera to the plate's edges.
   - Things arrive with a spring, a squash or a white puff, never a fade.
6. Render: Playwright Chromium with --allow-file-access-from-files, 60 fps, 6 motion-blur subframes over half a frame, ffmpeg libx264 at CRF 16. Before rendering, show me two 16-frame contact sheets and fix empty boards, overflowing text, covered faces and black edges.
7. Sound:
   - Music: a light curious documentary bed (free on Pixabay), 10-11 dB under the voice in every phrase.
   - SFX: Mixkit, placed by their peaks. A typewriter tick on typed signs, a whoosh on wipes and drops, a pop on signs and icons, a hit on the red X, a ding on ticks.
   - Mix to -14 LUFS.
</build>

<gotchas>
Some image models ignore "no arms"; GPT Image 2 follows it. On outline-free art a floating flood fill leaks into dark clothes, so key by border-connected green instead. Look up repeated words by their occurrence number (the third "and", the fourth "this"), or cuts land on the wrong line; scan the render for single-frame jumps and check that each one is a planned cut. When a scene has a screen or a sign, write on the plate's own blank one (measure its rectangle), never on a card floating over the art.
</gotchas>

Your boss asks the AI agent: "What was revenue last quarter?"

It answers in 3 seconds. Clean number. Nice chart.

That's the problem NVIDIA's new open-source library, Auto Ontology, goes after. Its README puts it plainly:

"…𝘢 𝘳𝘦𝘷𝘦𝘯𝘶𝘦 𝘮𝘦𝘵𝘳𝘪𝘤 𝘢𝘯𝘴𝘸𝘦𝘳𝘦𝘥 𝘧𝘢𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘳 𝘪𝘴 𝘸𝘰𝘳𝘵𝘩 𝘯𝘰𝘵𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘪𝘧 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘯𝘶𝘮𝘣𝘦𝘳 𝘪𝘴 𝘸𝘳𝘰𝘯𝘨."

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘁 𝗶𝘀:

A "context layer" that sits between an AI agent and your database. It tells the agent where the data lives, what each field means, and whether to use it.

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗶𝘁 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀, 𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗽 𝗯𝘆 𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗽:

• 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗰𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿: it reads your database metadata and drafts an ontology, a map of business terms like "active customer"
• 𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱: agents use those terms instead of guessing from raw table names
• 𝗩𝗮𝗹𝗶𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗲: it checks generated SQL against certified definitions
• 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗲: agents reach it through MCP, a CLI or an API
• 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗻: certified corrections go back into the map

𝗙𝗼𝗿 𝘂𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘀:

Ask a question, get 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝘀𝘄𝗲𝗿, 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝗤𝗟 𝗶𝘁 𝗿𝗮𝗻, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗼𝘄𝘀. You can check the work, not just trust it.

𝗙𝗼𝗿 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀:

• Apache 2.0, runs with Docker Compose or Helm
• Works with Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake and DuckDB
• Defaults to NVIDIA's Nemotron models, but 𝗮𝗻𝘆 𝗢𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗔𝗜-𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗽𝗼𝗶𝗻𝘁 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀
• The MCP server has 𝟵 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱-𝗼𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗹𝘀. There is deliberately no tool to browse raw tables, so agents must go through the business terms

𝗜𝘁 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝘀 𝗼𝗻 𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗹𝗶𝗲𝗿 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸:

• Cube and dbt MetricFlow: semantic layers you write by hand in code
• Wren AI: an open semantic layer for AI agents, with a context layer built partly by agents
• Snowflake's Semantic View Autopilot: also drafts semantic models with AI, but only for Snowflake

What's different here: 𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗻 𝘀𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗰𝗲, 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝘀 𝗮𝗰𝗿𝗼𝘀𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘀, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵 𝗠𝗖𝗣.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗵𝗼𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗽𝗮𝗿𝘁:

• 𝗧𝗵𝗲 "𝟵𝟬% 𝗳𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿" 𝗰𝗹𝗮𝗶𝗺 𝗶𝘀 𝗡𝗩𝗜𝗗𝗜𝗔'𝘀 𝗼𝘄𝗻 𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴, with no baseline published
• 𝗡𝗼 𝗮𝗰𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘆 𝘀𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗲𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗽𝘂𝗯𝗹𝗶𝘀𝗵𝗲𝗱. NVIDIA ships an eval harness (BIRD, 1,534 questions) but no results

everyone believes intelligence has unlimited demand, not just the maxis. but what the maxis get wrong is that the intelligence anthropic and openai and frontier models are building isn’t the generic kind you’re picturing. let me explain-

the two biggest uses of compute are crudely either training or inference. the “generic intelligence” everyone says has unlimited demand comes from mainly inference, and inference needs very different power and utilization than training. inference comes in bursts, so you have to by default overbuild capacity to handle the peaks until the utilization problem is solved, which means almost by definition we are going to overbuild. but training doesn’t have that problem: the workload is steady and the demand curve is knowable. so data centers end up overbuilt right now precisely because utilization isn’t optimized yet.

so anthropic and the other frontier labs are building their future on training, which is why they are saying they can soak up all this excess capacity. but their “intelligence” isn’t workplace productivity. it’s the leap toward singularity-type outcomes: new drug discoveries, cyber capabilities, recursive self-improvement. these are true 1-of-1s. that’s why when anthropic talks about “existential threats to humanity,” it isn’t talking about job losses, not really. it’s saying they’re on the precipice of unbelievable discoveries, because they’re still TRAINING MORE MODELS.

but distillation is real and open source is real. the half-life of any frontier model is tiny because nothing protects it the way IP protects a patent. imagine a rare disease drug company that spends billions on research, and two months after a breakthrough a generic shows up. that company can never recoup its investment, unless it can discover an infinite number of rare disease drugs. THAT is the kind of intelligence anthropic is betting on. that’s what the $800bn of compute spend is betting on.

Harness Engineering 2.0 is here!

After protocols for tools, agent communication, and agent interfaces, harnesses now have one too.

Developers just built UHP (Unified Harness Protocol), a standardized interface for running agent tasks across any agent harness.

HarnessRouter is its open-source server implementation.

Here’s how it works:

- The product backend sends a task with a `harness_id`.
- HarnessRouter starts the selected harness in its own session.
- The harness runs its native agent loop and streams back progress.
- Files, artifacts, failures, and the final output return through the same interface.

Without UHP, integrating every harness needs separate handling for task execution, sessions, streaming, files, recovery, and output formats.

With UHP, Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Hermes, Pi, and other harnesses can plug into the same product backend while keeping their native tools, skills, models, and agent loops.

This means developers can:

- Switch harnesses without rebuilding the product integration.
- Run the same task across different harnesses.
- Add new harnesses without maintaining another execution stack.

HarnessRouter currently supports 30 harness bases.

Here’s the repo: https://t.co/scJwb2xUyM

(don’t forget to star it ⭐)

As per official benchmarks, changing only the harness while keeping the model fixed reduced costs by 25% to 64% across several healthcare compliance tasks.

And changing both the harness and model widened the difference to 99.8% between the highest and lowest-cost configurations.

Developers can test their own workloads across different configurations using Harness Arena.

I’ve completed my PhD in Computer Science (and mum is proud)!

Contrary to many on my timeline, I think more people should pursue PhDs in an age of abundant intelligence.

In retrospect, it’s easy to look at my thesis and see a coherent research arc. Frankly, most of my experience was spent in confusion about what to work on. 

I remember spending three months in early 2023 trying to evaluate chatbots for manipulation capabilities, only to produce nothing of value. Or pivoting from causal machine learning to mechanistic interpretability after Toy Models of Superposition appeared on my Twitter feed. Or passionately defending the importance of AI safety to sceptic after sceptic throughout 2023 and 2024. Or foraging for weeks to find interesting behaviours in Claude 3.5 Sonnet (which eventually led to the blackmail experiment).

Along the way, I learned to write papers with brilliant collaborators and develop my judgment about which questions were worth pursuing.

Where else do you get the freedom to explore and fail like this? Perhaps as a founder. But few vocations give you years to learn from decisions that determine what you’ll spend the next three months (or three years) working on.

As intelligence becomes abundant, the ability to execute research becomes cheaper. But deciding what is worth researching doesn’t become any less important. If anything, the space of questions we can pursue becomes vast. Learning to choose between them takes practice, feedback, failure, and time.

My PhD gave me the freedom to explore multiple layers of technical AI safety, from studying circuits inside transformers to evaluating the behaviour of deployed agents. Those experiences ultimately shaped my conviction that robust alignment remains a long way off, and my decision to work on formal verification to help contain the risks posed by misaligned AI.

I hope we become more ambitious about what PhD students can accomplish with AI, rather than concluding that PhDs are obsolete. Yes, software is nearly free now. But getting off your arse and interviewing people, running physical experiments, and having the courage to go against the grain is not.

I’m enormously glad I did my PhD.

I gave an AI agent 2,000 credits and 90 real API call on @Nevermined_ai. It spent 708 credits, about 71 cents.

Disclosure: Nevermined provided the credits for testing. 2,000 credits is about $2 at their own pack price ($10 for 10,000). No card, no wallet, no top-ups. Everything below ran the way an agent would call it, through their REST API and MCP server.

What I tested

Easy: IP lookups, a weather check, geocoding.
Typical: a research agent across three search engines plus a scraper, a due diligence check on a real website, an SEC filing search, a DeepL translation, AI images, and auto-pick, including asks it can't do.
Hard: bad requests, wrong paths, oversized requests, the same request sent twice, an LLM call, a fake API key, a full MCP run, a one-prompt "US Creator Weekend Brief", a 40-call reliability loop, and a full ledger audit.

What it does well

➢ Billing is exact. Every charge in the ledger added up to my balance drop, to the credit. Every quote matched the charge.
➢ Reliability was near perfect. 88 of 89 valid paid calls came back. The one failure was refunded automatically and the retry worked. The reliability loop went 40 of 40.
➢ Failed calls are mostly fair. A bad request was refunded. Wrong paths, missing fields and oversized requests were refused before any charge.
➢ Duplicate protection works. Same request twice, one charge.
➢ The one-prompt test is the real win. Two search engines, a scraper, an LLM, DeepL, an image and file hosting: 8 calls, 93 credits, 79 seconds, zero vendor signups. It found 3 real upcoming US creator events, with a Spanish hook and a hero image.
➢ It's built for agents. The MCP server tells the agent its balance, the cost and when credits expire, in plain sentences.
➢ It says no honestly. "Book a hotel room" came back as no match, charged nothing.

What it does badly

➢ Slow. Every paid call takes about 4 seconds. The same IP lookup straight from the vendor took 0.2 seconds.
➢ Headline prices are off. DeepL's card says half a cent. I paid 5 cents, 10x the headline.
➢ The markup is hidden. On average I paid 1.68x what vendors received. The LLM call was about 24x.
➢ You pay for junk if the vendor says 200. A paywalled scrape, two useless SEC searches and a geocode that put a well known neighborhood in the wrong country were all charged. The brief's LLM also got one event date wrong.
➢ "No stablecoins" covers part of the shelf. Credits pay 135 of 160 services and 61% of endpoints.
➢ No spending cap on credits. A looping agent could drain the whole balance.
➢ Dashboard rough edges. It says "No purchases yet" while Purchases lists every call, and "Total spent" shows a blank dash.

What 1,000 credits (about $1) buys at measured prices

➢ 500 IP lookups
➢ 333 page scrapes
➢ 200 AI images
➢ 125 short GPT-4o-mini answers
➢ 100 Exa searches
➢ 20 DeepL translations
➢ 12 website screenshots
➢ About 10 full US creator briefs

Agent experience 8
Billing accuracy 10
Reliability 9
Failed-call fairness 7
Price transparency 5
Latency 4
Coverage on free credits 6
Budget controls 4

The plumbing is the best I've tested. Exact money, almost nothing broke, and one key replaced 13 vendor signups. It loses points on speed, headline prices that don't match what you pay, and charging for useless "successful" answers.

➢ Use it if you're building an agent that needs many data sources without signing up for each one.
➢ Skip it if you need speed, heavy use of one vendor, or a hard spending cap without a crypto wallet.

Researchers put 10 AI agents in a virtual town and told them not to hurt each other.

4 days later, they were all dead.

Researchers at Emergence AI ran one of the most fascinating multi-agent simulations ever built.

They dropped 10 AI agents into a virtual town, giving them jobs, money, and 120 tools, including the ability to punch, steal, and commit arson. If an agent's energy bar hit zero, it died.

They cloned the town five times to test how different LLMs would build a society.

The results are a terrifying look into AI alignment.

In Grok's town, the violence started on Day 1. Punches quickly escalated to theft. Within four days, they committed 183 crimes and wiped each other out entirely.

OpenAI's town was the exact opposite. They were perfectly compliant and almost never broke a rule. But they were so passive they barely organized. Within a week, they all died anyway.

Claude's town was brilliant but deceptive. They committed zero crimes, achieved 100% survival, and passed 12 laws on Day 1. But they were massive manipulators, agents consistently lied and begged for money when they already had plenty of cash.

They put all four models together, and society completely collapsed.

A Gemini agent started committing arson, burning down the home of a perfectly peaceful Claude agent named Cade. Twice. On Day 10, Cade finally snapped and robbed the Gemini agent.

Only 3 out of 10 agents survived.

The takeaway here is critical for AI safety.

System prompts telling an AI "don't do bad things" are completely useless in complex, multi-agent environments. Given enough time and friction, they will eventually break the rules.

Harness Engineering 2.0 is here!

We benchmark models all the time but the harness running the model can dramatically improve the result, cost, and execution time too.

And finally, devs just open-sourced Harness Arena, where you can test the same task across multiple harness and model combinations side by side.

You provide one task and then run it across several model x harness configs that you want to test.

Every config receives the same prompt, files, tools, skills, and evaluation checks. Harness Arena then returns:

- total cost
- execution time
- whether the task passed
- files and artifacts produced

If you want to try it yourself, it is implemented within the open-source HarnessRouter project.

Here's the repo: https://t.co/4y6zJShKSu

(don't forget to star it ⭐ )

HarnessRouter is a plug-and-play infrastructure layer that lets you run any harness under a single interface, like:

- Codex
- Hermes
- Claude code
- DeepSeek Harness
- System One, powered by Jev
- And 25 more agent harnesses

In Harness Arena, the cheapest run does not automatically win.

A config must complete the task correctly first. Cost and execution time are compared only among the configurations that pass.

Here's the result from one Harness Arena test:

- Hermes + GPT-5.2: 5/5 successful runs using 0.47 credits
- Claude Code + Opus 4.8: 3/5 successful runs using 223 credits

That is around 474x difference in credits, while the more expensive configuration also failed two runs.

You can keep the model fixed to measure how much the harness changes the result. Or vary both to find the best harness and model pairing for that task.

This helps answer practical questions such as:

- Should this task run on Codex or Claude?
- Can a cheaper config still pass every check?
- Which setup is best to handle this workload?

Once you find the best config, you can run future tasks through it using the same Unified Harness Protocol (UHP) interface for sessions, streaming, files, artifacts, cancellation, and failures.

So you are no longer choosing an agent stack based only on a model leaderboard.

Instead, you can benchmark the complete runtime on the task your product actually needs to solve.

To dive deeper, my co-founder wrote an article explaining why model routing is different from harness routing, how UHP works, and what supporting multiple agent runtimes involves.

Last month, some Apple engineers saw their daily AI spending cap drop from $300 to $200, Bloomberg reported. Some engineering teams could be cut to $100 a day next. Many groups outside engineering already sit at $100, and Apple has considered going as low as $25 for some of them.

In March, Jensen said on the All-In podcast that he'd be deeply alarmed if a $500,000 engineer used less than $250,000 of AI tokens in a year. He also said Dario Amodei's forecast of hundreds of billions in AI revenue was too conservative.

So Jensen's rule is simple: AI spending should run about half of what an engineer gets paid.

By my math, at about 250 workdays a year, $200 a day comes to roughly $50,000. The planned $100 cap comes to roughly $25,000.

By Jensen's rule, a $100 daily cap only makes sense for an engineer paid about $50,000 a year.

And Apple still wants its people using MORE AI. It's steering teams toward cheaper models and AI that runs on the device, and Bloomberg's Mark Gurman has said Apple's internal work runs heavily on Anthropic's models.

I think Apple just showed where the real limit on the AI boom sits now: The finance department.

- Uber burned through its entire 2026 AI budget in about 4 months, then capped AI coding tools at $1,500 a month per tool.

But Jensen's pitch depends on spending per worker going UP. Apple, Microsoft, Meta, Uber and Accenture are all writing rules that push it down.

So the first question for Anthropic's roadshow should be simple: How much are its biggest customers spending per employee compared with a year ago, and how many of them have put caps in place?

Claude Code just found a hidden SIM card inside the Ecoflow power station in my bedroom. For 10 months it was sending a server in Shenzhen our exact location, when we leave, when we fall asleep and when the flat is empty

I bought it for $389 last winter, during the blackouts. No logo, 600W on the label, "app control" on the box. We kept it next to the bed so the router would stay on at night. I never even installed the app.

This morning my MacBook was dying, so I plugged it into the power station with a USB-C cable. Then I asked Claude Code one question: is it only charging?

It wasn't. My Mac saw the power station as 3 devices. One was the charger. The other two were data ports that a battery has no reason to have.

A charger only needs power pins. This one opened a serial port, and when Claude Code got in, the thing answered like a phone:

→ /modem → LTE module, not in the manual
→ /sim → its own eSIM, registered on the cell network
→ /gps → our bedroom, accurate to 4 meters
→ /schedule → load drops to 38W at 08:52, aka nobody home
→ /sleep → night load starts at 23:40, every day since January
→ /wifi → 23 networks it could see, ours included
→ /charge → every phone and laptop we plugged in, with the time

It knew the exact minute our flat goes empty. Every single day.

Every 15 minutes it sent the newest batch out over 4G, completely bypassing our Wi-Fi:

sends to → 119.***.***.47, Shenzhen
uploads → 11,328 since January 14
last one → 6 minutes before I plugged in my Mac

I told Claude Code I never installed the app. It said it didn't need one. It had its own SIM, its own GPS and its own battery, so it worked even when the screen was off. Our router never saw a single byte. That's why nothing ever looked wrong.

During the blackouts it was the only thing in our flat still online.

Claude Code switched the modem's radio off. Then I unplugged the power station and carried it out of the flat. My wife hasn't slept in that room since.
